meta.title: Water Under Your Feet
meta.skill_frame: Use facts in the passage to work out something it does not say directly.

reader.tone: Adult subject. Plain sentences. The lesson must not make the reader feel small.

source.basis: USGS Water Science School, 'Aquifers and Groundwater'.
source.attribution: U.S. Geological Survey, Water Science School, 'Aquifers and Groundwater', https://www.usgs.gov/water-science-school/science/aquifers-and-groundwater, accessed 2026-10-26. U.S. federal government work; public domain in the U.S.

session.difficulty_basis: Clue distance and one hidden link, held level across the band.

script_overrides.near_copy_2: Say it in your own words. One sentence is enough.

passage.part_1: A huge amount of water exists in the ground below your feet. People all over the world make use of it. It is found in usable amounts only in certain places underground, and those places are called aquifers. An aquifer is rock or sand that holds water and can pass it to wells and springs. The wet area beneath the water table is the aquifer, and aquifers are huge storehouses of water. Wells are drilled into them, and pumps pull the water out. Rain and snow add water back over time, and that process is called recharge. Some aquifers are deep underground.
passage.part_2: The upper surface of the water-filled area is called the water table, and below it every space in the rock is full. Dig a hole in wet sand at the beach. Water will rise in it until it reaches the same level as the ocean. The water table can rise and fall with the weather, and pumping too much water too fast draws it down. A well can then yield less water or run dry, and a neighbor's well on the same aquifer can fail for the same reason. Wells must reach down to the water. That is why well depth matters.

tutor_only.confirm: Right. Rock or sand that holds water and lets it move.
tutor_only.correct_reason: The passage defines an aquifer in one sentence.
tutor_only.tell: An aquifer is rock or sand. It holds water and lets water pass through it.
help: Find the sentence that begins with the words an aquifer is.
The definition names two jobs: holding water and letting it move.
tutor_only.core_idea: An aquifer is rock or sand that holds water and lets water move through it.
accept_ideas: rock or sand that holds water
a layer that holds water and lets it move
an underground place where water is stored

if_they_say.when: the student says an aquifer is a kind of pipe
if_they_say.ask: A pipe carries water in a closed tube. The passage names rock and sand. What do they do?

items.prompt: The passage says rain and snow recharge an aquifer. What does recharge mean here?

tutor_only.confirm: Yes. It means water is added back to the aquifer.
tutor_only.correct_reason: Recharge is defined by the sentence before it: rain and snow add water back over time.
tutor_only.tell: Recharge means refilling. Rain and snow add water back to the aquifer after it is pumped.
help: Read the sentence before the word recharge.
That sentence says what rain and snow do to the aquifer.
tutor_only.core_idea: Recharge means water is added back to the aquifer.

if_they_say.when: the student says recharge means pumping water out
if_they_say.ask: Pumping takes water out. Which direction does rain and snow move the water?

items.prompt: Pumping too much water can make a neighbor's well run dry. Why?

tutor_only.confirm: Right. Both wells pull from the same aquifer, so the level drops for both.
tutor_only.correct_reason: The passage says pumping lowers the water table and that a neighbor on the same aquifer is affected.
tutor_only.tell: A well does not own its water. Both wells draw from one aquifer, so heavy pumping lowers the water for both.
help: Look at the end of the passage, where pumping is described.
Look at where the neighbor's water comes from.
tutor_only.core_idea: Because both wells use the same aquifer, so pumping lowers the water for both.
accept_ideas: the water table drops for both wells
the neighbor's well pulls from the same water

if_they_say.when: the student says the neighbor's well is broken
if_they_say.ask: The passage does not say the well breaks. What happens to the water level?

items.prompt: Where does the water stop in a hole dug in wet sand at the beach?

tutor_only.confirm: Yes. At the same level as the ocean.
tutor_only.correct_reason: The passage states that the water in the beach hole stops level with the ocean.
tutor_only.tell: The water in the hole rises to the ocean's level. That level is the water table.
help: Find the sentence about the beach hole.
It compares the water level in the hole to something nearby.
tutor_only.core_idea: At the same level as the ocean.
accept_ideas: at the level of the ocean
the same height as the ocean
not_required: how long the hole takes to fill

if_they_say.when: the student says the hole fills to the top
if_they_say.ask: The passage names a level. Which level does it name?

items.prompt: Why should people who use wells care about recharge?

tutor_only.confirm: Yes. Without recharge, the water they pump is not replaced.
tutor_only.correct_reason: The two parts connect: wells take water out, recharge puts water back.
tutor_only.tell: Recharge is the refilling. A well that pumps faster than the aquifer refills will run low.
help: Think about what happens to a store of water when water only leaves.
Connect the pumping sentences to the recharge sentence.
tutor_only.core_idea: Because recharge is how the water they pump is replaced.
accept_ideas: without it the aquifer runs low
the water they use is not added back

if_they_say.when: the student says recharge is another word for rain
if_they_say.ask: Rain is one source. The passage gives recharge a job. What is that job?
